**How to apply:** Reuse `experiments/13_.../Fable/render_fable.py` as the renderer template; pass an
absolute output prefix (Blender resolves relative paths against its own cwd). See
[[craftbot-project-overview]] if it exists.

model with sloped members; rotated boxes cannot be plumb/mitre cut and always fail the overlap check at joints.

with extra sections (reference comparison, structural improvements).

# The Segal Method — Extracted Notes

**Source:** *The Architects' Journal*, Special Issue: "The Segal Method", 5 November 1986, pp. 31–68. Written by Jon Broome (self-builder and joint architect with Walter Segal on the Lewisham self-build housing schemes). Extracted from `THE SEGAL METHOD - color.pdf`.

**Scope of source:** Describes the essential features and implications of Walter Segal's timber-frame self-build method, following the self-build sequence from planning through to finishes. Cover photo: two-storey Segal house with pitched roof, exposed dark timber frame, white infill panels, external spiral stair and raised deck.

---

## Contents of the source document

- Walter Segal's approach
- The essential method
- 1 General arrangement
- *The planning process:* 2 Modular grid · 3 Layout drawings · 4 Structural layout · 5 Calculations · 6 Framing drawings · 7 Schedule of materials · 8 Catalogue of elements · 9 Building instructions
- *The building process:* 10 Foundations · 11 Structural frame · 12 Roof · 13 Floors · 14 External walls · 15 Windows · 16 Partitions · 17 Ceilings · 18 Stairs and other features · 19 Services
- The future

---

## Key dimensions quick reference

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Modular grid (tartan) — panel width | 600 mm or 1200 mm |
| Tartan grid — structural zone / joint gap | 50 mm |
| Structural thickness (columns, panels) | commonly 50 mm |
| Column depth | >50 mm, sized to suit structural requirements; stands partly outside grid |
| Structural depth (floor/roof zone) | ~200 mm |
| Max column spacing | up to 6 modules apart in either direction |
| Max structural bay | 3.85 m in either direction (accommodates most domestic rooms) |
| Foundation pad | ~600 × 600 mm plan, ~900 mm deep (or to suit local ground/bearing) |
| Concrete bases per house | ~18 for 3-bed bungalow; ~12 for two-storey house |
| Roof shingle ballast | 40 mm layer of 20 mm diameter shingle |
| Roof membrane | 3-layer bituminous felt, bonded to each other, NOT bonded to deck |
| Wall/partition core | 50 mm woodwool slab |
| Ceiling boards | 600 mm wide plasterboard (1200 mm boards cut in half on site) |
| Window panes | fixed + sliding glass panes up to ~1 m² |
| Window pane clearance | 1 mm gap between fixed and sliding panes |
| Design life | 60 years (extendable through adaptation) |
| First house (Highgate, 1962) | built in 2 weeks, materials cost £800 (~£6500 in 1986) |

---

## Walter Segal's approach

- **Origin (1962):** Segal built a temporary house in his Highgate garden for his family while the main house was rebuilt. Completed in **two weeks** for a materials cost of **£800** (~£6500 at 1986 prices). It still stood in 1986.
- Private clients then commissioned **two dozen or so private houses** in England and Ireland over the next 15 years. A students' residence was designed/built by students in **Stuttgart, 1983**. A house was built by this method in **Australia in 1980** after two long telephone calls. Other architects (e.g. **David Lea** — vicarage at Melling near Liverpool; housing at Churt, Surrey) applied Segal's ideas.
- The method uses **widely available building materials put together in an open-ended way** — the speed and economy of open-system building without the monotony/inflexibility of a closed system.
- Segal **rethought common technical problems from first principles** (e.g. flat-roof failures, condensation), avoiding the defects that afflict much system-built housing.

### A humane architecture
- The houses are not monumental or massive; they show concern for comfort and utility, respond to occupants, and **can be easily altered** — "an architecture of liberation."
- Not to be confused with "prefab": quality as harmony of form, fitness, purpose (per Christopher Alexander), together with being ordinary and unremarkable.
- Essentially an **updated version of medieval timber-framing** using basic products of industry and commonly understood skills. Echoes of a pre-industrial age; could also demonstrate a post-industrial one.

### A potential for self-build
- Simplification lets non-experts build a house and non-architects control design.
- **1971:** first self-build — a school teacher near **Woodbridge, Suffolk** built his own Segal-designed house after watching the carpenter and deciding he could do it himself.
- **1978 Lewisham (south-east London):** 14 families from the council's housing waiting/transfer lists built their own houses. A second Lewisham scheme was nearing completion in 1986. No one excluded by circumstances — houses built by people in their 60s and by a single mother.
- Advantages of self-build under this method:
  - Each family builds its own house **individually from start to finish**, setting its own programme (avoids the pressure of communal rota schemes; parents and children take part — a family enterprise).
  - Self-builders do nearly all operations themselves (no subcontractors) — saves money, avoids coordination problems.
  - Houses need not be identical; the method allows design amendment **during construction** (e.g. move a window to catch a view).
  - Houses can be extended: one family added a bedroom over **three weekends for £1200**.
  - Progressive development can cut initial cost and extend useful life beyond the **60-year design life**.

### Housing standards
- Essential simplicity ≠ highest conventional performance (e.g. sound insulation measures) — but houses are **detached**, so no neighbour noise anyway (typical Segal lateral thinking).
- Thermal insulation standards improved over the method's development. Segal understood there is a point beyond which elaboration negates the advantages of simplicity.
- Segal experimented with new materials/techniques only when based on knowledge or experience — no untried materials of unproven performance.
- The method developed from temporary to permanent houses, from one-off contractor-built designs to self-built houses with high user control.

---

## The essential method (principles list)

- An **attitude of mind rather than a system of construction**; rigorous simplification of the whole building process from design to completion.
- Process rethought from **first principles** to handle fundamentals: tolerances, thermal and moisture movement.
- Elements reduced to essentials — maximum economy of material and effort.
- Uses **readily available materials and techniques** (not special manufacture) → market competition on price and availability; the method can absorb improvements in techniques and materials.
- Standard materials assembled on site **in their market sizes** → minimal on-site production, minimal waste.
- Building boards (plasterboard, woodwool slabs) form the enclosure within a **framework of standard timber sections**. (The approach could also apply to steel for frame and infill.)
- Materials chosen for performance and cost; workable with **simple hand power tools**; easily handled size and weight.
- Organised on a **modular grid determined by the sizes of standard materials**.
- **Dry jointing only** (bolts and screws) — wet trades (bricklaying, plastering) eliminated.
- Foundations and groundworks reduced to a minimum.
- Buildable by **one person with basic carpentry skills**, except possibly services and roofing.
- Quick and economical construction.
- **Simple documentation:** small freehand A4 diagrams of layout and structure, standard junction details, schedule of materials, set of instructions.
- The **schedule of materials** combines bill of quantities, specification and order list → accurate ordering and cost control from the outset.
- Architect's role includes quantity surveyor and, ideally, engineer.
- The process is **"transparent"** — understandable and controllable by someone without experience; a novice can plan the layout and do the work.
- Buildings feel light and optimistic, are **very adaptable and easy to extend**.
- Produces one- and two-storey buildings with flat or pitched roofs, courtyards, split levels, double-height spaces.

---

## The planning process

### 1 General arrangement (fig. 18)
Cutaway isometric of a two-storey Segal building showing all numbered elements in place: foundations (10) as discrete pads below posts; structural frame (11) of posts and beams; roof (12); floors (13); external walls (14); windows (15); partitions (16); ceilings (17); stairs (18); services (19); modular grid (2); structural layout (4). Order of description ≈ sequence of execution.

### 2 Modular grid
- Both structural frame and infill walls/partitions planned on a **modular "tartan" grid**: wide bands = panel width (**600 mm or 1200 mm**, from standard board sizes), narrow bands = structural thickness (**commonly 50 mm**).
- Tartan grid lets **corners and columns (generally 50 mm thick)** occur at any grid position **without cutting panels**. Trade-off: a 50 mm gap is left at every joint position in a straight wall (more jointing material) — accepted because grid planning + uncut standard panels outweigh it.
- **Columns are deeper than 50 mm**, so they stand partly outside the grid: placed outside the building where possible, or projecting from partitions; never set longways within the grid (would require cutting panels).
- Client can plan on **squared paper**; drawings can be simple tools (self-builder's floor plan shown drawn on graph paper, fig. 20).
- **Walls carry no load** → walls, doors, windows can go anywhere on either floor and can be changed at any stage, even during construction (fig. 21).
- Vertical dimensions controlled the same way: infill panel height + structural depth of frame. **Ceiling panels fit between joists without cutting** (fig. 22; ~200 mm structural depth shown with 50/600/50 tartan spacing).

### 3 Layout drawings
- Two or three simple **A4 freehand diagrams**: plan and elevations showing positions of walls and openings (figs. 23–24, Lewisham self-build example). Superfluous information omitted.
- Used together with calculations, framing drawings, schedule of materials, catalogue of elements, and building instructions.
- In practice layout drawings are referred to only occasionally once the frame is up and the modular arrangement is legible in the building itself.

### 4 Structural layout
- Structure is a **post and beam frame** (fig. 25a), *not* stud-wall panel construction (fig. 25b).
- A frame is less timber-efficient than panels but: **far smaller/cheaper foundations**, and great planning freedom and adaptability.
- Design order (figs. 26a–c): **plan first** (partition layout decided first), then frame designed to suit the plan; column layout follows partition layout; columns may sit partially outside the tartan grid.
- Columns spaced **up to six modules apart in either direction** — optimum span before beam deflection becomes critical. Gives a structural bay of up to **3.85 m** in either direction (fits most domestic rooms). Composite beams or trusses possible for larger spans.

### 5 Calculations
- Once the structural layout is fixed, the structure is calculated for adequacy and the most economical form, integrating structure with plan and constructional discipline. **Joints get particular attention** (most critical part).
- Building Regulations submission typically includes: dead/imposed load tabulation, wind loads, bending and deflection of critical beams and joists at floor and roof levels, critical columns (axial + bending), joints, wind overturning, soil bearing pressures.
- A set is about **a dozen pages** (example shown: floor joist bending calculation, fig. 27).

### 6 Framing drawings
- Prepared after calculation check; again **A4 freehand diagrams** (ground floor framing plan and sections A-A, B-B shown, figs. 28–29) with the dimensional information needed to construct the frame.
- Typical set: foundation layout, plans at roof levels, sections, joint details — **about eight sheets altogether**.

### 7 Schedule of materials
- Detailed list of all materials for the particular building: each component described with **size, length, finish, and location** in the building, with diagrammatic annotations (fig. 30 example ~10 pages for a house).
- Combination of bill of quantities + specification, prepared by the architect; describes each piece of material accurately.
- Also used as the **ordering list and delivery checklist**; yields a very accurate cost at the outset that will not vary significantly on completion.

### 8 Catalogue of elements
- Standard document per building: series of simple **A4 diagrams of standard details** of each element and how they go together to form the basic shell (fig. 31 shows typical partition/wall junction details: battens, woodwool, plasterboard, screw sizes, e.g. Ex 25×25 battens, 50×50 blocks, 12.7 mm plasterboard, 75 mm No 8 screws).
- With the typical junction arrangements, buildings of many shapes and sizes can be formed.

### 9 Building instructions
- Final documentation element: simple **step-by-step description of the building process**, annotated with diagrams (fig. 32 example: making the main cross-frames — "BE METHODICAL, BE CAREFUL": mark all posts and beams, mark out all joints, mark out notches, cut to length, check actual depth of planed timber, lay out posts and beams for each frame).
- Inexperienced self-builders attend a short course of ~**12 evening sessions**: method + documentation (slides, models, drawings) and workshop sessions building confidence with hand and power tools, making typical joints, basic plumbing and wiring.
- On site people learn by example and pass on information; at Lewisham regular meetings monitor progress. Architect available by phone in the evening and visits weekly (weekends). Mindset: careful, methodical, think operations through, plan ahead.

---

## The building process

### 10 Foundations
- Essential feature: **the building stands above the ground on posts** rather than being built *in* the ground.
- Foundations are **separate in-situ concrete bases below each post position**: dig hole (building inspector approves bottom), fill with concrete, cap with a **concrete paving slab set at a slight fall**. Posts stand on the slabs **on a piece of lead** forced into the end grain by the building's weight — seals the post against moisture.
- Pad size: about **600 × 600 mm** (or to suit soil bearing pressure), **~900 mm deep** or to suit local ground conditions (fig. 33).
- Topsoil below the building is removed and replaced with **gravel within a border of paving slabs**; **no concrete oversite slab**.
- Concrete quantities small → dug by hand, placed by wheelbarrow (fig. 34): avoids ready-mix and machine excavation costs, suits restricted sites, keeps groundworks self-buildable.
- Foundations built **at whatever ground level exists — no site levelling**. Works on sloping sites without significant cost increase; trees are not damaged by nearby buildings.
- Typical count: **3-bed bungalow ≈ 18 bases; two-storey house ≈ 12**. Isolated pads are less extensive/expensive than continuous foundations under loadbearing walls.
- **Levels are taken and each post cut to length** so floors come out precisely level when frames are erected. The undercroft below the building is a useful storage "cellar" (fig. 35).
- **Posts are not anchored to the foundations** — the building's weight keeps them in place. Once frames are erected, post positions can be adjusted for distance and square **independently of the foundations** (fig. 36: check modular dimensions between frames, check diagonals for square; lead between posts and foundations). Accurate setting-out of foundations is therefore unnecessary — removing an operation inexperienced builders find difficult.
- **Short bored piles** are an economical alternative (no ground beams needed); quick, good for poor soils.

### 11 Structural frame
- Like medieval timber framing: a number of **cross-frames with rigid joints, assembled flat on the ground, raised into position, braced together** (fig. 37: frame assembled flat on the oversite deck).
- Erection sequence (figs. 38–41): frames assembled flat, stacked in order of erection; first frame erected and secured with **struts into the ground**; remaining frames raised one at a time and **temporarily braced to the first with timbers to be used later in construction**, until permanent bracing is fixed. Temporary braces removed one at a time to adjust frames for square and position.
- Timber: **slender sections of stress-graded, imported softwood, pressure treated against rot**.
- **Rigid joints formed with galvanised steel bolts** (in place of medieval mortice-and-tenon with pegs). Form/proportion of the frame has more in common with steel than traditional timber framing; slender sections keep frames light enough to handle by hand.
- **Portal frame behaviour** (fig. 44): rigid joints resist wind in the plane of the frame, but unlike a conventional portal there is a **tie beam at floor level** that eliminates horizontal reactions at the column base — this is what allows the building to stand on the ground unanchored, with no critical foundation tolerances.
- Frames are rigid in one direction; in the other direction they are **braced together**: the floor is fixed to form a **rigid horizontal plate** transferring wind forces to the bracing position (fig. 45). (The roof could act as a plate too.)
- **Bracing:** generally one cross-brace bay per floor level near the centre of the building (figs. 41, 42, 45). Single-storey houses can use **knee braces below floor level** (fig. 43), avoiding the planning limitation of a fixed braced bay above floor.
- **Bolt sizing:** bolt size from joint load and timber type; bolt sizes dictate minimum spacing between bolts and to timber edges (fig. 46).
- **Beams:** centre frames get **double beams**, edge frames **single beams**, so all beams carry a similar load (fig. 49).
- **Joists** fixed between erected frames at roof and floor levels; **spacing and thickness conform to the modular grid** (fig. 47: joists of modular thickness, fixed at modular spacing).
- **Beams and joists have the same depth**: joists fixed with a bearer on the side of beams so that **undersides of beams and joists are at the same level** (figs. 50–51) → nothing projects below ceiling level, all wall panels the same height. Possible because beam timber is much stronger than joist timber.
- Later-use timbers are fixed temporarily to posts as a **working platform** for fixing upper joists — **no scaffolding needed** (fig. 48).
- Frames can cantilever (fig. 52); deflection then governs.

### 12 Roof
- Roof built **immediately after the frame** so all later work happens under cover (fig. 54).
- **Flat roof preferred**: quick, easy, economical, fits any plan shape, allows extension in any direction. Segal rethought flat-roof construction from first principles to avoid its classic failures:
  - **Membrane laid loose** ("tablecloth principle", fig. 55): waterproof layer draped over the roof, **not fixed to deck and not fixed at edges** → structural/deck movement is not transferred to the membrane (no cracks/leaks); membrane free to expand/contract without wrinkles or edge tears. (Many large flat roofs now use this 'loose lay' principle.)
  - **Generous overhang all round** protects the building — creates a "microclimate" of shelter (fig. 53). The **roof outlet is the only penetration**, positioned in the overhang so the joint is fail-safe.
  - **Deck:** woodwool slabs **laid loose on the joists, without falls**; dimensioned to avoid cutting slabs; laid level (fig. 56).
  - **With a perimeter upstand the roof is wet at all times** — keeps the membrane at a relatively even temperature.
  - **Membrane:** conventional **three-layer bituminous felt build-up** (economical), layers hot-bitumen bonded **to one another but not to the deck**. Hot-bonding is a job for a professional roofer; cold bitumen or single-layer butyl rubber membrane could make it fully self-build (eliminating all subcontractors).
  - **Ballast:** membrane weighted with **40 mm of 20 mm shingle**, which also keeps direct sunlight off the felt (fig. 56).
  - **Edge detail (fig. 57):** felt carried up and over a perimeter upstand and turned down over the fascia; if the roof outlet blocks, water simply overflows the upstand harmlessly (and signals the blockage). Edge wedged by a **two-piece timber capping fixed through spacer blocks below the felt edge** — no fixings through the felt itself, so it can expand/contract freely.
  - **Insulation** commonly at ceiling level; void above ceiling ventilated via the loose construction (avoids interstitial condensation). Also very easy to insulate on top as an **upside-down (inverted) roof**.

### 13 Floors
- Fixed after the roof. Generally conventional **tongued-and-grooved softwood boarding on joists** (fig. 58). (Chipboard would be vulnerable to weather since walls aren't up yet.)
- Ground floor is **raised above ground** → insulated against extra heat loss; the raised floor gives a full-extent storage **undercroft**; services run easily in this space.
- **Insulation laid between joists on panels which can be removed** for service access (fig. 59: t&g flooring on joists; panels and insulation on battens fixed to joists, liftable out for access).

### 14 External walls
- Fixed floors provide the working platform. External walls are **non-structural infill clamped into the structural frame with bolts** (bolt heads visible outside, fig. 60).
- Wall = **sandwich of readily available building boards**: insulating and structural core + weatherproof external finish + decorative internal finish.
- **Segal's clothes analogy (fig. 61):** vest (comfortable inside) + sweater (warmth) + raincoat (dry outside). Like loose-fitting clothes, the layers fit **loosely** so air circulates between them and condensation cannot build up. **No reliance on a vapour barrier** (whose integrity can't be guaranteed) — safe, at the cost of higher ventilation heat losses.
- **Typical build-up:** fully compressed **fibre-cement panel with enamel finish (e.g. Glasal) outside**, **painted plasterboard inside**, **50 mm woodwool slab core** between. Materials selected per situation (thermal insulation, design life); panel sizes selected to eliminate cutting and waste.
- Optional extra layers: **urethane foam** for thermal performance; **plastic laminate** inside for washable splashback around a bath.
- **Assembly (fig. 62):** panels clamped together with **timber battens bolted through with three spun galvanised steel bolts** per joint. Battens engage a **sole plate at the bottom** and the **structural joist at the top**; **blocks fixed top and bottom establish the tartan grid position** (fig. 63).
- **Joint is not sealed** (fig. 65): a **weep hole at the bottom of each joint** drains it and ventilates the wall. Elements simply lap over one another → conventional tolerances irrelevant; large tolerance makes the wall easy to build (fig. 64 plan of junction: structural column 50; weatherproof external finish; insulation and structural core; decorative internal finish; corners formed with battens screwed into blocks; infill panels clamped into frame with battens bolted together; 50/600/50 tartan dimensions).
- **Finish as you go:** plasterboard painted and external battens stained before/during assembly — decorating is one of the first operations, not the last.

### 15 Windows
- Fixed after wall panels to make the building weathertight (fig. 66).
- Philosophy: **assemble easily available materials on site to make a window** rather than buying a factory component — avoids tolerance/modular coordination problems, single-source dependence, delivery delays; cuts costs (no transport or factory overheads).
- **Construction (fig. 69):** windows are sheets of glass with **polished edges sliding horizontally in a track of two aluminium angles**, held by timber beads, all within a timber window lining. One angle is fixed **through a spacer washer (tap washer)** to form a **drainage slot** in the track. The angles provide the sliding surface and act as spacer between fixed and sliding panes (**1 mm clearance** so panes slide past one another). Glass **lubricated by running a wax candle** along the pane edge before fixing. Rain falling on the sliding pane runs behind the angle and out through the slot; dry glazing tape seats fixed glass.
- Very adaptable: fixed and opening panes **up to about one metre square** in great variety — storey-height glazing (fig. 67), horizontal strip glazing (fig. 70), varied shapes (Melling vicarage by David Lea, fig. 68). **Double windows** = a second set constructed inside the first.
- Chief disadvantage: **not airtight**. Remedy: clear plastic channel pushed onto the edge of one pane closes the 1 mm gap; foam strip seals the part of the drainage slot not needed below the fixed pane. Conventional windows can also be incorporated.

### 16 Partitions
- Built once weathertight (fig. 71). Same clamping principle as external walls: panels clamped into the frame with timber battens.
- Build-up: **structural core with internal finish both sides** — commonly **50 mm woodwool slab + painted plasterboard each side** (fig. 72). Extra layers possible (e.g. **softboard as pinboard**).
- Engage a **sole plate at bottom** and **structural joist at top**, blocks top and bottom set the tartan grid. Partition running perpendicular to joists needs a **filler piece at its top**.
- **Corners/junctions** formed with timber battens as for external walls. Because the wall is overlapping elements clamped together, boards forming the finish can be **offset off the modular grid at corners** to accommodate their thickness — avoiding cut panels (fig. 73).
- **Door linings made on site** and incorporated in the wall. Fixings for shelving/fittings available at **every batten position**.

### 17 Ceilings
- Fixed after partitions (fig. 74). Commonly **painted plasterboard laid between the joists on battens**; boards **600 mm wide**, only trimmed in length (1200 mm boards cut in half on site). Rooms ≥ 6 modules wide need two boards end-to-end with a **cover strip** at the joint.
- Ceiling below the roof can hold **extra insulation**; boards **lift out for access to services**.
- **Fire resistance:** ceiling below a first floor achieves a **modified half-hour fire resistance** via **sacrificial timber linings fixed to the joists** (fig. 75) — the linings char in a fire, leaving structural joists unaffected. Satisfies Building Regulations; relies on timber's predictable burn rate (thickness ↔ time to burn through).

### 18 Stairs and other features
- Stairs/steps designed to **avoid complicated setting-out, angle cutting, and jointing**: treads supported on **hangers** (fig. 76), **posts** (fig. 77), or **cantilever beams** (fig. 78). Timber members **lap over one another at right angles**.
- Externally, **hardwood — generally keruing —** for treads and walkways (decay resistant).
- The basic structure adapts to many features: **pergola, porch, seat (fig. 80), bay window (fig. 79), trellis, veranda (fig. 81), walkway, balustrade**. Great variety of form, colour and detail is possible within the modular discipline.

### 19 Services
- Construction incorporates **voids in roofs, floors and walls** for services, all accessible by **unscrewing a batten or lifting out a panel** (fig. 83).
- **Lighting** wiring in the **ceiling/roof void**; switch drops run **in the 50 mm spaces between wall panels at joints**.
- **Power ring main** in the **floor void**, rising to socket outlets **at batten positions**; switches and sockets can be positioned on any batten by cutting a cabling hole in it (fig. 82).
- **Pipework** (heating flow/return, gas, hot and cold water) runs in the **floor void**; **waste pipes** suspended in the space **below the ground floor**.

---

## The future (implications)

- Roles of tradesmen and professionals altered by rigorous simplification of the process.
- Buildings become genuinely adaptable/flexible — "**tools**" to be put to different uses rather than fixed edifices.
- Maintenance attitudes change (easy replacement of worn parts).
- Financing could change: build a **small basic initial house capable of easy upgrading and extension**.
- Kit-of-parts approach → far greater resident choice in public and private developments.
- Many more people could build their own homes with control, variety and satisfaction. (Stockholm City Council has run self-build departments since the 1920s; 10,000-family waiting list in 1986.)
- Choice: an alternative to subsidised mass housing and anonymous mass-produced private housing. Potential for unemployed people to build (self-confidence → employment); small-scale self-regulating communities of self-built houses on vacant urban sites.
- Walter Segal became the only living architect (to the author's knowledge) named in the London A–Z: **Segal Close, SE23** (figs. 84–85); **Walter's Way** to be listed the following year.

---

## Buildings referenced (figures 1–17)

| Fig | Building | Notes |

| 9 | House in Western Australia, 1980 | AJ 19.8.81 p338 |
| 10 | House at Lewisham, London, 1980 | First Lewisham scheme (AJ 17.12.80 p1185) |

23	|---|---|

25	| Tartan grid — structural zone / joint gap | 50 mm |

28	| Structural depth (floor/roof zone) | ~200 mm |

43	
44	## Walter Segal's approach
45	
46	- **Origin (1962):** Segal built a temporary house in his Highgate garden for his family while the main house was rebuilt. Completed in **two weeks** for a materials cost of **£800** (~£6500 at 1986 prices). It still stood in 1986.
47	- Private clients then commissioned **two dozen or so private houses** in England and Ireland over the next 15 years. A students' residence was designed/built by students in **Stuttgart, 1983**. A house was built by this method in **Australia in 1980** after two long telephone calls. Other architects (e.g. **David Lea** — vicarage at Melling near Liverpool; housing at Churt, Surrey) applied Segal's ideas.
48	- The method uses **widely available building materials put together in an open-ended way** — the speed and economy of open-system building without the monotony/inflexibility of a closed system.
49	- Segal **rethought common technical problems from first principles** (e.g. flat-roof failures, condensation), avoiding the defects that afflict much system-built housing.
50	
51	### A humane architecture
52	- The houses are not monumental or massive; they show concern for comfort and utility, respond to occupants, and **can be easily altered** — "an architecture of liberation."
53	- Not to be confused with "prefab": quality as harmony of form, fitness, purpose (per Christopher Alexander), together with being ordinary and unremarkable.
54	- Essentially an **updated version of medieval timber-framing** using basic products of industry and commonly understood skills. Echoes of a pre-industrial age; could also demonstrate a post-industrial one.
55	
56	### A potential for self-build
57	- Simplification lets non-experts build a house and non-architects control design.
58	- **1971:** first self-build — a school teacher near **Woodbridge, Suffolk** built his own Segal-designed house after watching the carpenter and deciding he could do it himself.
59	- **1978 Lewisham (south-east London):** 14 families from the council's housing waiting/transfer lists built their own houses. A second Lewisham scheme was nearing completion in 1986. No one excluded by circumstances — houses built by people in their 60s and by a single mother.
60	- Advantages of self-build under this method:
61	  - Each family builds its own house **individually from start to finish**, setting its own programme (avoids the pressure of communal rota schemes; parents and children take part — a family enterprise).
62	  - Self-builders do nearly all operations themselves (no subcontractors) — saves money, avoids coordination problems.
63	  - Houses need not be identical; the method allows design amendment **during construction** (e.g. move a window to catch a view).
64	  - Houses can be extended: one family added a bedroom over **three weekends for £1200**.
65	  - Progressive development can cut initial cost and extend useful life beyond the **60-year design life**.
66	
67	### Housing standards
68	- Essential simplicity ≠ highest conventional performance (e.g. sound insulation measures) — but houses are **detached**, so no neighbour noise anyway (typical Segal lateral thinking).
69	- Thermal insulation standards improved over the method's development. Segal understood there is a point beyond which elaboration negates the advantages of simplicity.
70	- Segal experimented with new materials/techniques only when based on knowledge or experience — no untried materials of unproven performance.
71	- The method developed from temporary to permanent houses, from one-off contractor-built designs to self-built houses with high user control.
72	
73	---
74	
75	## The essential method (principles list)
76	
77	- An **attitude of mind rather than a system of construction**; rigorous simplification of the whole building process from design to completion.
78	- Process rethought from **first principles** to handle fundamentals: tolerances, thermal and moisture movement.
79	- Elements reduced to essentials — maximum economy of material and effort.
80	- Uses **readily available materials and techniques** (not special manufacture) → market competition on price and availability; the method can absorb improvements in techniques and materials.
81	- Standard materials assembled on site **in their market sizes** → minimal on-site production, minimal waste.
82	- Building boards (plasterboard, woodwool slabs) form the enclosure within a **framework of standard timber sections**. (The approach could also apply to steel for frame and infill.)
83	- Materials chosen for performance and cost; workable with **simple hand power tools**; easily handled size and weight.
84	- Organised on a **modular grid determined by the sizes of standard materials**.
85	- **Dry jointing only** (bolts and screws) — wet trades (bricklaying, plastering) eliminated.
86	- Foundations and groundworks reduced to a minimum.
87	- Buildable by **one person with basic carpentry skills**, except possibly services and roofing.
88	- Quick and economical construction.
89	- **Simple documentation:** small freehand A4 diagrams of layout and structure, standard junction details, schedule of materials, set of instructions.
90	- The **schedule of materials** combines bill of quantities, specification and order list → accurate ordering and cost control from the outset.
91	- Architect's role includes quantity surveyor and, ideally, engineer.
92	- The process is **"transparent"** — understandable and controllable by someone without experience; a novice can plan the layout and do the work.
93	- Buildings feel light and optimistic, are **very adaptable and easy to extend**.
94	- Produces one- and two-storey buildings with flat or pitched roofs, courtyards, split levels, double-height spaces.

99	
100	### 1 General arrangement (fig. 18)
101	Cutaway isometric of a two-storey Segal building showing all numbered elements in place: foundations (10) as discrete pads below posts; structural frame (11) of posts and beams; roof (12); floors (13); external walls (14); windows (15); partitions (16); ceilings (17); stairs (18); services (19); modular grid (2); structural layout (4). Order of description ≈ sequence of execution.

103	### 2 Modular grid
104	- Both structural frame and infill walls/partitions planned on a **modular "tartan" grid**: wide bands = panel width (**600 mm or 1200 mm**, from standard board sizes), narrow bands = structural thickness (**commonly 50 mm**).
105	- Tartan grid lets **corners and columns (generally 50 mm thick)** occur at any grid position **without cutting panels**. Trade-off: a 50 mm gap is left at every joint position in a straight wall (more jointing material) — accepted because grid planning + uncut standard panels outweigh it.
106	- **Columns are deeper than 50 mm**, so they stand partly outside the grid: placed outside the building where possible, or projecting from partitions; never set longways within the grid (would require cutting panels).
107	- Client can plan on **squared paper**; drawings can be simple tools (self-builder's floor plan shown drawn on graph paper, fig. 20).
108	- **Walls carry no load** → walls, doors, windows can go anywhere on either floor and can be changed at any stage, even during construction (fig. 21).
109	- Vertical dimensions controlled the same way: infill panel height + structural depth of frame. **Ceiling panels fit between joists without cutting** (fig. 22; ~200 mm structural depth shown with 50/600/50 tartan spacing).

112	- Two or three simple **A4 freehand diagrams**: plan and elevations showing positions of walls and openings (figs. 23–24, Lewisham self-build example). Superfluous information omitted.
113	- Used together with calculations, framing drawings, schedule of materials, catalogue of elements, and building instructions.
114	- In practice layout drawings are referred to only occasionally once the frame is up and the modular arrangement is legible in the building itself.
115	
116	### 4 Structural layout
117	- Structure is a **post and beam frame** (fig. 25a), *not* stud-wall panel construction (fig. 25b).
118	- A frame is less timber-efficient than panels but: **far smaller/cheaper foundations**, and great planning freedom and adaptability.
119	- Design order (figs. 26a–c): **plan first** (partition layout decided first), then frame designed to suit the plan; column layout follows partition layout; columns may sit partially outside the tartan grid.
120	- Columns spaced **up to six modules apart in either direction** — optimum span before beam deflection becomes critical. Gives a structural bay of up to **3.85 m** in either direction (fits most domestic rooms). Composite beams or trusses possible for larger spans.
121	
122	### 5 Calculations
123	- Once the structural layout is fixed, the structure is calculated for adequacy and the most economical form, integrating structure with plan and constructional discipline. **Joints get particular attention** (most critical part).
124	- Building Regulations submission typically includes: dead/imposed load tabulation, wind loads, bending and deflection of critical beams and joists at floor and roof levels, critical columns (axial + bending), joints, wind overturning, soil bearing pressures.
125	- A set is about **a dozen pages** (example shown: floor joist bending calculation, fig. 27).
126	
127	### 6 Framing drawings
128	- Prepared after calculation check; again **A4 freehand diagrams** (ground floor framing plan and sections A-A, B-B shown, figs. 28–29) with the dimensional information needed to construct the frame.
129	- Typical set: foundation layout, plans at roof levels, sections, joint details — **about eight sheets altogether**.
130	
131	### 7 Schedule of materials
132	- Detailed list of all materials for the particular building: each component described with **size, length, finish, and location** in the building, with diagrammatic annotations (fig. 30 example ~10 pages for a house).
133	- Combination of bill of quantities + specification, prepared by the architect; describes each piece of material accurately.
134	- Also used as the **ordering list and delivery checklist**; yields a very accurate cost at the outset that will not vary significantly on completion.
135	
136	### 8 Catalogue of elements
137	- Standard document per building: series of simple **A4 diagrams of standard details** of each element and how they go together to form the basic shell (fig. 31 shows typical partition/wall junction details: battens, woodwool, plasterboard, screw sizes, e.g. Ex 25×25 battens, 50×50 blocks, 12.7 mm plasterboard, 75 mm No 8 screws).
138	- With the typical junction arrangements, buildings of many shapes and sizes can be formed.
139	
140	### 9 Building instructions
141	- Final documentation element: simple **step-by-step description of the building process**, annotated with diagrams (fig. 32 example: making the main cross-frames — "BE METHODICAL, BE CAREFUL": mark all posts and beams, mark out all joints, mark out notches, cut to length, check actual depth of planed timber, lay out posts and beams for each frame).
142	- Inexperienced self-builders attend a short course of ~**12 evening sessions**: method + documentation (slides, models, drawings) and workshop sessions building confidence with hand and power tools, making typical joints, basic plumbing and wiring.
143	- On site people learn by example and pass on information; at Lewisham regular meetings monitor progress. Architect available by phone in the evening and visits weekly (weekends). Mindset: careful, methodical, think operations through, plan ahead.
144	
145	---
146	
147	## The building process
148	
149	### 10 Foundations
150	- Essential feature: **the building stands above the ground on posts** rather than being built *in* the ground.
151	- Foundations are **separate in-situ concrete bases below each post position**: dig hole (building inspector approves bottom), fill with concrete, cap with a **concrete paving slab set at a slight fall**. Posts stand on the slabs **on a piece of lead** forced into the end grain by the building's weight — seals the post against moisture.
152	- Pad size: about **600 × 600 mm** (or to suit soil bearing pressure), **~900 mm deep** or to suit local ground conditions (fig. 33).
153	- Topsoil below the building is removed and replaced with **gravel within a border of paving slabs**; **no concrete oversite slab**.
154	- Concrete quantities small → dug by hand, placed by wheelbarrow (fig. 34): avoids ready-mix and machine excavation costs, suits restricted sites, keeps groundworks self-buildable.
155	- Foundations built **at whatever ground level exists — no site levelling**. Works on sloping sites without significant cost increase; trees are not damaged by nearby buildings.
156	- Typical count: **3-bed bungalow ≈ 18 bases; two-storey house ≈ 12**. Isolated pads are less extensive/expensive than continuous foundations under loadbearing walls.
157	- **Levels are taken and each post cut to length** so floors come out precisely level when frames are erected. The undercroft below the building is a useful storage "cellar" (fig. 35).
158	- **Posts are not anchored to the foundations** — the building's weight keeps them in place. Once frames are erected, post positions can be adjusted for distance and square **independently of the foundations** (fig. 36: check modular dimensions between frames, check diagonals for square; lead between posts and foundations). Accurate setting-out of foundations is therefore unnecessary — removing an operation inexperienced builders find difficult.
159	- **Short bored piles** are an economical alternative (no ground beams needed); quick, good for poor soils.
160	
161	### 11 Structural frame
162	- Like medieval timber framing: a number of **cross-frames with rigid joints, assembled flat on the ground, raised into position, braced together** (fig. 37: frame assembled flat on the oversite deck).
163	- Erection sequence (figs. 38–41): frames assembled flat, stacked in order of erection; first frame erected and secured with **struts into the ground**; remaining frames raised one at a time and **temporarily braced to the first with timbers to be used later in construction**, until permanent bracing is fixed. Temporary braces removed one at a time to adjust frames for square and position.
164	- Timber: **slender sections of stress-graded, imported softwood, pressure treated against rot**.
165	- **Rigid joints formed with galvanised steel bolts** (in place of medieval mortice-and-tenon with pegs). Form/proportion of the frame has more in common with steel than traditional timber framing; slender sections keep frames light enough to handle by hand.
166	- **Portal frame behaviour** (fig. 44): rigid joints resist wind in the plane of the frame, but unlike a conventional portal there is a **tie beam at floor level** that eliminates horizontal reactions at the column base — this is what allows the building to stand on the ground unanchored, with no critical foundation tolerances.
167	- Frames are rigid in one direction; in the other direction they are **braced together**: the floor is fixed to form a **rigid horizontal plate** transferring wind forces to the bracing position (fig. 45). (The roof could act as a plate too.)
168	- **Bracing:** generally one cross-brace bay per floor level near the centre of the building (figs. 41, 42, 45). Single-storey houses can use **knee braces below floor level** (fig. 43), avoiding the planning limitation of a fixed braced bay above floor.
169	- **Bolt sizing:** bolt size from joint load and timber type; bolt sizes dictate minimum spacing between bolts and to timber edges (fig. 46).
170	- **Beams:** centre frames get **double beams**, edge frames **single beams**, so all beams carry a similar load (fig. 49).
171	- **Joists** fixed between erected frames at roof and floor levels; **spacing and thickness conform to the modular grid** (fig. 47: joists of modular thickness, fixed at modular spacing).
172	- **Beams and joists have the same depth**: joists fixed with a bearer on the side of beams so that **undersides of beams and joists are at the same level** (figs. 50–51) → nothing projects below ceiling level, all wall panels the same height. Possible because beam timber is much stronger than joist timber.
173	- Later-use timbers are fixed temporarily to posts as a **working platform** for fixing upper joists — **no scaffolding needed** (fig. 48).
174	- Frames can cantilever (fig. 52); deflection then governs.
175	
176	### 12 Roof
177	- Roof built **immediately after the frame** so all later work happens under cover (fig. 54).
178	- **Flat roof preferred**: quick, easy, economical, fits any plan shape, allows extension in any direction. Segal rethought flat-roof construction from first principles to avoid its classic failures:
179	  - **Membrane laid loose** ("tablecloth principle", fig. 55): waterproof layer draped over the roof, **not fixed to deck and not fixed at edges** → structural/deck movement is not transferred to the membrane (no cracks/leaks); membrane free to expand/contract without wrinkles or edge tears. (Many large flat roofs now use this 'loose lay' principle.)
180	  - **Generous overhang all round** protects the building — creates a "microclimate" of shelter (fig. 53). The **roof outlet is the only penetration**, positioned in the overhang so the joint is fail-safe.
181	  - **Deck:** woodwool slabs **laid loose on the joists, without falls**; dimensioned to avoid cutting slabs; laid level (fig. 56).
182	  - **With a perimeter upstand the roof is wet at all times** — keeps the membrane at a relatively even temperature.
183	  - **Membrane:** conventional **three-layer bituminous felt build-up** (economical), layers hot-bitumen bonded **to one another but not to the deck**. Hot-bonding is a job for a professional roofer; cold bitumen or single-layer butyl rubber membrane could make it fully self-build (eliminating all subcontractors).
184	  - **Ballast:** membrane weighted with **40 mm of 20 mm shingle**, which also keeps direct sunlight off the felt (fig. 56).
185	  - **Edge detail (fig. 57):** felt carried up and over a perimeter upstand and turned down over the fascia; if the roof outlet blocks, water simply overflows the upstand harmlessly (and signals the blockage). Edge wedged by a **two-piece timber capping fixed through spacer blocks below the felt edge** — no fixings through the felt itself, so it can expand/contract freely.
186	  - **Insulation** commonly at ceiling level; void above ceiling ventilated via the loose construction (avoids interstitial condensation). Also very easy to insulate on top as an **upside-down (inverted) roof**.
187	
188	### 13 Floors
189	- Fixed after the roof. Generally conventional **tongued-and-grooved softwood boarding on joists** (fig. 58). (Chipboard would be vulnerable to weather since walls aren't up yet.)
190	- Ground floor is **raised above ground** → insulated against extra heat loss; the raised floor gives a full-extent storage **undercroft**; services run easily in this space.
191	- **Insulation laid between joists on panels which can be removed** for service access (fig. 59: t&g flooring on joists; panels and insulation on battens fixed to joists, liftable out for access).
192	
193	### 14 External walls
194	- Fixed floors provide the working platform. External walls are **non-structural infill clamped into the structural frame with bolts** (bolt heads visible outside, fig. 60).
195	- Wall = **sandwich of readily available building boards**: insulating and structural core + weatherproof external finish + decorative internal finish.
196	- **Segal's clothes analogy (fig. 61):** vest (comfortable inside) + sweater (warmth) + raincoat (dry outside). Like loose-fitting clothes, the layers fit **loosely** so air circulates between them and condensation cannot build up. **No reliance on a vapour barrier** (whose integrity can't be guaranteed) — safe, at the cost of higher ventilation heat losses.
197	- **Typical build-up:** fully compressed **fibre-cement panel with enamel finish (e.g. Glasal) outside**, **painted plasterboard inside**, **50 mm woodwool slab core** between. Materials selected per situation (thermal insulation, design life); panel sizes selected to eliminate cutting and waste.
198	- Optional extra layers: **urethane foam** for thermal performance; **plastic laminate** inside for washable splashback around a bath.
199	- **Assembly (fig. 62):** panels clamped together with **timber battens bolted through with three spun galvanised steel bolts** per joint. Battens engage a **sole plate at the bottom** and the **structural joist at the top**; **blocks fixed top and bottom establish the tartan grid position** (fig. 63).
200	- **Joint is not sealed** (fig. 65): a **weep hole at the bottom of each joint** drains it and ventilates the wall. Elements simply lap over one another → conventional tolerances irrelevant; large tolerance makes the wall easy to build (fig. 64 plan of junction: structural column 50; weatherproof external finish; insulation and structural core; decorative internal finish; corners formed with battens screwed into blocks; infill panels clamped into frame with battens bolted together; 50/600/50 tartan dimensions).
201	- **Finish as you go:** plasterboard painted and external battens stained before/during assembly — decorating is one of the first operations, not the last.
202	
203	### 15 Windows
204	- Fixed after wall panels to make the building weathertight (fig. 66).
205	- Philosophy: **assemble easily available materials on site to make a window** rather than buying a factory component — avoids tolerance/modular coordination problems, single-source dependence, delivery delays; cuts costs (no transport or factory overheads).
206	- **Construction (fig. 69):** windows are sheets of glass with **polished edges sliding horizontally in a track of two aluminium angles**, held by timber beads, all within a timber window lining. One angle is fixed **through a spacer washer (tap washer)** to form a **drainage slot** in the track. The angles provide the sliding surface and act as spacer between fixed and sliding panes (**1 mm clearance** so panes slide past one another). Glass **lubricated by running a wax candle** along the pane edge before fixing. Rain falling on the sliding pane runs behind the angle and out through the slot; dry glazing tape seats fixed glass.
207	- Very adaptable: fixed and opening panes **up to about one metre square** in great variety — storey-height glazing (fig. 67), horizontal strip glazing (fig. 70), varied shapes (Melling vicarage by David Lea, fig. 68). **Double windows** = a second set constructed inside the first.
208	- Chief disadvantage: **not airtight**. Remedy: clear plastic channel pushed onto the edge of one pane closes the 1 mm gap; foam strip seals the part of the drainage slot not needed below the fixed pane. Conventional windows can also be incorporated.
209	
210	### 16 Partitions
211	- Built once weathertight (fig. 71). Same clamping principle as external walls: panels clamped into the frame with timber battens.
212	- Build-up: **structural core with internal finish both sides** — commonly **50 mm woodwool slab + painted plasterboard each side** (fig. 72). Extra layers possible (e.g. **softboard as pinboard**).
213	- Engage a **sole plate at bottom** and **structural joist at top**, blocks top and bottom set the tartan grid. Partition running perpendicular to joists needs a **filler piece at its top**.
214	- **Corners/junctions** formed with timber battens as for external walls. Because the wall is overlapping elements clamped together, boards forming the finish can be **offset off the modular grid at corners** to accommodate their thickness — avoiding cut panels (fig. 73).
215	- **Door linings made on site** and incorporated in the wall. Fixings for shelving/fittings available at **every batten position**.
216	
217	### 17 Ceilings
218	- Fixed after partitions (fig. 74). Commonly **painted plasterboard laid between the joists on battens**; boards **600 mm wide**, only trimmed in length (1200 mm boards cut in half on site). Rooms ≥ 6 modules wide need two boards end-to-end with a **cover strip** at the joint.
219	- Ceiling below the roof can hold **extra insulation**; boards **lift out for access to services**.
220	- **Fire resistance:** ceiling below a first floor achieves a **modified half-hour fire resistance** via **sacrificial timber linings fixed to the joists** (fig. 75) — the linings char in a fire, leaving structural joists unaffected. Satisfies Building Regulations; relies on timber's predictable burn rate (thickness ↔ time to burn through).
221	
222	### 18 Stairs and other features
223	- Stairs/steps designed to **avoid complicated setting-out, angle cutting, and jointing**: treads supported on **hangers** (fig. 76), **posts** (fig. 77), or **cantilever beams** (fig. 78). Timber members **lap over one another at right angles**.
224	- Externally, **hardwood — generally keruing —** for treads and walkways (decay resistant).
225	- The basic structure adapts to many features: **pergola, porch, seat (fig. 80), bay window (fig. 79), trellis, veranda (fig. 81), walkway, balustrade**. Great variety of form, colour and detail is possible within the modular discipline.
226	
227	### 19 Services
228	- Construction incorporates **voids in roofs, floors and walls** for services, all accessible by **unscrewing a batten or lifting out a panel** (fig. 83).
229	- **Lighting** wiring in the **ceiling/roof void**; switch drops run **in the 50 mm spaces between wall panels at joints**.
230	- **Power ring main** in the **floor void**, rising to socket outlets **at batten positions**; switches and sockets can be positioned on any batten by cutting a cabling hole in it (fig. 82).
231	- **Pipework** (heating flow/return, gas, hot and cold water) runs in the **floor void**; **waste pipes** suspended in the space **below the ground floor**.
232	
233	---
234	
235	## The future (implications)
236	
237	- Roles of tradesmen and professionals altered by rigorous simplification of the process.
238	- Buildings become genuinely adaptable/flexible — "**tools**" to be put to different uses rather than fixed edifices.
239	- Maintenance attitudes change (easy replacement of worn parts).
240	- Financing could change: build a **small basic initial house capable of easy upgrading and extension**.
241	- Kit-of-parts approach → far greater resident choice in public and private developments.
242	- Many more people could build their own homes with control, variety and satisfaction. (Stockholm City Council has run self-build departments since the 1920s; 10,000-family waiting list in 1986.)
243	- Choice: an alternative to subsidised mass housing and anonymous mass-produced private housing. Potential for unemployed people to build (self-confidence → employment); small-scale self-regulating communities of self-built houses on vacant urban sites.
244	- Walter Segal became the only living architect (to the author's knowledge) named in the London A–Z: **Segal Close, SE23** (figs. 84–85); **Walter's Way** to be listed the following year.
245	
246	---
247	
248	## Buildings referenced (figures 1–17)
249	
250	| Fig | Building | Notes |
251	|---|---|---|
252	| 1 | Segal's house at Highgate, London, 1962 | The original two-week prototype (AJ 20.6.84 p35) |
253	| 2 | Holiday house at Ballygarrett, Ireland, 1968 | AJ 30.9.70 p769 |
254	| 3 | House at North Chailey, Sussex, 1969 | AJ 30.9.70 p773 |
255	| 4 | Children's home at Singleton, Sussex, 1972 | |
256	| 5 | House at Mill Hill, London, 1975 | AJ 20.4.77 p716 |
257	| 6 | Student's self-build, Stuttgart, 1983 | AJ 27.7.83 p32 |
258	| 7 | Vicarage at Melling, nr Liverpool, by David Lea | AJ 26.11.75 p1121; also Churt, Surrey housing by Lea |
259	| 8 | House at Woodbridge, Suffolk, 1971 | First self-build (AJ 3.9.75 p458) |
260	| 9 | House in Western Australia, 1980 | AJ 19.8.81 p338 |
261	| 10 | House at Lewisham, London, 1980 | First Lewisham scheme (AJ 17.12.80 p1185) |
262	| 11 | House in second Lewisham scheme, 1986 | AJ 25.1.84 p37 |
263	| 12 | Family building | Parents and children on site |
264	| 13 | Extension under construction | Bedroom added in 3 weekends for £1200 |
265	| 14 | House at Yelling, Cambridgeshire, 1970 | Also the interior on the title page (AJ 30.9.70 p772) |
266	| 15 | House at Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, 1980 | |
267	| 16 | House at Halstead, Essex, 1969 | AJ 30.9.70 p770 |
268	| 17 | Sheltered housing for old people at Churt, Surrey, 1972 | Designed by David Lea |
269	
270	---
271	
272	## Key diagrams (figure index)
273	
274	| Fig | Content |
275	|---|---|
276	| 18 | General arrangement cutaway isometric: all elements 2–19 located on a two-storey frame |
277	| 19 | Tartan grid bird's-eye: 600 panel bands, 50 structural bands; corners formed without cutting panels; column depth outside grid; gap at joints in straight walls |
278	| 20 | Self-builder's first-floor plan on graph paper (bedrooms, bath, stair, bracing marked) |
279	| 21 | Walls/openings placeable in any position on either floor |
280	| 22 | Section: ceiling panel fits between joists without cutting; ~200 structural depth; 50/600/50 grid |
281	| 23–24 | Layout drawings: elevations with window schedule; ground-floor plan |
282	| 25a/b | Frame structure vs NOT structural panels |
283	| 26a–c | Partition layout decided first → column layout follows → columns partially outside tartan grid; 3.85 m max bay |
284	| 27 | Sample floor-joist bending calculation (loads, section modulus, bending stress check) |
285	| 28–29 | Framing drawings: ground-floor framing plan; sections A-A and B-B with bracing |
286	| 30 | Schedule of materials sample page (timber sizes, lengths, finishes, prices) |
287	| 31 | Catalogue of elements: typical partition/wall junction details |
288	| 32 | Building instructions sample: making main cross-frames, marking and cutting sequence |
289	| 33 | Foundation isometric: pad ~600 sq, 900 deep; paving slab cap with fall; gravel oversite in slab border; posts cut to suit ground floor level |
290	| 34 | Photo: hand-mixing/barrowing concrete into pad |
291	| 35 | Photo: house on sloping site, undercroft "cellar" |
292	| 36 | Frames adjusted independently of foundations; check diagonals and modular dimensions; lead between post and foundation |
293	| 37 | Cross-frame assembled flat on oversite deck |
294	| 38–41 | Erection sequence: assembled flat → stacked in erection order → pushed up, strutted → temporarily braced together |
295	| 42–43 | Cross-bracing bay photo; knee braces below floor (single storey) |
296	| 44 | Portal frame diagram: rigid joints, floor-level tie beam eliminates base reactions |
297	| 45 | Wind bracing plan: frames rigid one way, rigid floor plates transfer forces to central braced bay |
298	| 46 | Bolted joint photo (bolt spacing) |
299	| 47 | Joists of modular thickness fixed at modular spacing |
300	| 49 | End frames single beams, centre frames double beams → equal load share |
301	| 50–51 | Bearer detail: beam and joist undersides at same level |
302	| 52 | Cantilevered frame |
303	| 53–55 | Roof overhang microclimate; tablecloth principle (membrane loose on deck, free to move) |
304	| 56 | Roof build-up: woodwool deck laid loose without falls; 3-layer felt bonded to each other only; shingle ballast |
305	| 57 | Roof edge: upstand, felt over fascia, two-piece timber capping on spacer blocks, overflow |
306	| 58–59 | T&g floor on joists; liftable insulation panels on battens between joists |
307	| 60–62 | Wall panel clamping; clothes analogy sandwich (raincoat/sweater/vest); exploded wall assembly with sole plate, battens, bolts, blocks at grid intersections |
308	| 63–65 | Grid blocks; plan of wall junction (50/600/50); unsealed weep-hole joint |
309	| 66–70 | Window fixing; storey-height glazing; Melling shapes; sliding glass track detail (aluminium angles, tap-washer spacer, 1 mm clearance, wax lubrication, drainage slot); strip glazing |
310	| 71–73 | Partition photo; partition sandwich (plasterboard/woodwool/plasterboard + optional pinboard); corner offset off grid to avoid cut panels |
311	| 74–75 | Ceiling boards between joists; sacrificial timber fire linings below first-floor joists |
312	| 76–81 | Stairs on hangers/posts/cantilevers; bay window, seat/porch, veranda |
313	| 82–83 | Power socket in wall batten; services section: lighting in roof void, switch drops in wall joint voids, ring main and pipework in floor void, waste below ground floor |
314	| 84–85 | Segal Close SE23 street sign and houses |
315	
316	---
317	
318	## Construction sequence summary (for procedural modelling)
319	
320	1. **Plan on tartan grid** (600 or 1200 mm modules, 50 mm structural bands); partitions first, then columns (≤6 modules apart, bay ≤3.85 m); columns outside grid/building or projecting from partitions.
321	2. **Foundations:** discrete concrete pads (~600 sq × 900 deep) capped with paving slabs at post positions only; gravel oversite; no levelling of site.
322	3. **Posts cut to length** per pad level; stand on lead pads, unanchored.
323	4. **Cross-frames** (post + beam + floor-level tie, bolted rigid joints) assembled flat, raised, plumbed, braced; joists (same depth as beams, modular spacing) on bearers; central cross-braced bay per floor; double beams at centre frames, single at edges.
324	5. **Roof immediately:** loose woodwool deck (no falls) → 3-layer felt loose-laid, edge upstand + overhang, single outlet in overhang → 40 mm shingle ballast.
325	6. **Floors:** t&g softwood on joists; liftable insulation panels between joists.
326	7. **External walls:** non-structural sandwich panels (Glasal / 50 mm woodwool / plasterboard) clamped by bolted battens to sole plate and joist; blocks set grid; unsealed weep-hole joints; finish as you go.
327	8. **Windows:** site-made horizontal-sliding glass in aluminium-angle tracks within timber linings; panes ≤ ~1 m².
328	9. **Partitions:** plasterboard/woodwool/plasterboard clamped panels, any grid position.
329	10. **Ceilings:** 600 mm plasterboard between joists on battens; sacrificial fire linings under first floors.
330	11. **Stairs/features:** lapped right-angle timber members on hangers/posts/cantilevers; keruing outside.
331	12. **Services** last: all in accessible voids (roof, wall joints, floor, undercroft).
